item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating recency, order and positional effects. [CETRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03047) distinguishes absolute order—how recently an interaction occurred—from relative ordering; its evidence concerns LLM recommenders, so transfer to BERT4Rec remains a hypothesis. [Guo et al., SIGIR 2026](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805712.3809738) report boundary-focused, U-shaped sensitivity in attention-based sequential recommenders that persists when collaborative signals move. This motivates controls distinguishing informative context from architectural position bias. [BERT4Rec’s original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690) establishes masked-item training to prevent target leakage through bidirectional attention.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: on training-history prefixes, fix the next-item target and candidate set; compare recent-item deletion against repeated count-matched random deletion, plus shuffling earlier interactions while preserving the latest item. Report paired target-rank deterioration and top-10 overlap, with confidence intervals from user-clustered bootstrap resampling. Explicitly distinguish compacting deletions, which change positions, from position-preserving replacements, which introduce a replacement-token effect. Use deterministic identity controls expecting unchanged scores, and deliberately corrupted MASK/readout controls to test whether the audit detects inference faults. For left-padded BERT4Rec, append the reserved MASK and read its final nonpadding representation. These are proposed controls, not a protocol established by the cited papers. Greater sensitivity demonstrates model dependence on context; it does not establish user intent, causal preference, or explanation faithfulness without further evidence."}
